#OTD in 1886, Theodore Roosevelt wrote a letter to his friend Henry Cabot Lodge. Buried in the middle of it is a word almost nobody notices.

He was 27, out of office and out of favor. He had held no post since his term in the New York Assembly ended in 1884. His first wife had died two and a half years earlier. He was ranching in Dakota Territory and running out of reasons to think anything better was coming.

Then an American newspaper editor named A. K. Cutting was arrested in Mexico — over a libel he had published on the Texas side of the border — and the papers filled with war talk.

Roosevelt saw an opening:

"I have written on to Secretary Endicott offering to try to raise some companies of horse riflemen out here in the event of trouble with Mexico. Will you telegraph me at once if war becomes inevitable?"

Then, a few lines further down:

"I think there is some good fighting stuff among these harum-scarum roughriders out here; whether I can bring it out is another matter."

Roughriders. August 1886. Twelve years before San Juan Heights.

No war came — diplomats settled the Cutting affair. Ten days later Roosevelt wrote Lodge again, half joking that he had written "as regards Mexico qua cowboy, not qua statesman," and then, wistfully: "If a war had come off I would surely have had behind me as utterly reckless a set of desperados as ever sat in the saddle."

Twelve years later he would raise one for real.

One note, since we would rather be accurate than quotable: you will often see Roosevelt quoted as offering "an entire regiment of cowboys." That phrase does not appear in anything he is known to have written. It traces to a Bismarck Tribune item reporting that "it is confidently believed Mr. Roosevelt would tender to the Government the services of an entire regiment of cowboys." What he actually wrote was better.

"Following the directions from the Interstate 94 exit to the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library, you might wonder if you've missed North Dakota's new tourist destination, so seamlessly does the building blend into the prairie. That's exactly the point."

Anna-Louise Jackson visited for Cowboy State Daily and wrote about the whole site: The Boardwalk out through the native grasses, the rooftop views across the 93 acres, and galleries that follow Roosevelt's life in chronological order.

She caught the thing the galleries were built to produce. A familiar refrain running through the exhibit, visitors starting the same unfinished sentence: "Oh wow, I had no idea that he ..."

That is the design brief in eight words.

Her account of the darkened room is the part worth reading twice. It holds one object: Roosevelt's diary, open to February 14, 1884, the day his wife and his mother died in the same house. He marked the page with a large X and wrote, "The light has gone out of my life."

Jackson also lands on something visitors rarely expect. In her words, you might be surprised by what you learn about "a politician who wouldn't neatly fit into either of today's dominant political parties."

Thank you, Cowboy State Daily, for making the drive.

#OTD in 1902, Theodore Roosevelt appointed Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. to the Supreme Court — a decision he came to regret.

The seat had belonged to Justice Horace Gray. Congress was out of session, so on August 11 Roosevelt issued a recess appointment.

Holmes was 61, chief justice of Massachusetts, and arguably the most original legal mind in the country. He had been wounded three times in the Civil War with the 20th Massachusetts.

Here is the part most people don't know: he never sat under that commission.

Holmes wanted to be confirmed first. Rather than take the bench on a recess appointment, he waited for the Senate — and Roosevelt withdrew it. "I feel that there is no necessity why you should be nominated in the recess," Roosevelt wrote him on August 21. The formal nomination went up on December 2, the Senate confirmed him two days later, and Holmes took the judicial oath on December 8, 1902.

Roosevelt believed he was getting an ally. He had a case coming — Northern Securities, the railroad combination built by J. P. Morgan, James J. Hill, and E. H. Harriman — and he wanted a Court that would let the government break it up.

On March 14, 1904, the government won, five votes to four. Holmes dissented.

Two and a half years later Roosevelt wrote to Henry Cabot Lodge: "From his antecedents, Holmes should have been an ideal man on the bench. As a matter of fact he has been a bitter disappointment, not because of any one decision but because of his general attitude."

Holmes was steadier about it. Writing in 1921, two years after Roosevelt's death, he said only: "We talked freely later, but it was never the same."

Holmes served nearly thirty years and retired at 90. He is remembered now as one of the great justices in American history — and as a reminder that judicial independence tends to show up where a president least wants it.

"It's the kind of destination where you can spend the morning spotting bison, enjoy an afternoon learning about western history, and end the day watching an incredible outdoor musical under the North Dakota sky."

That is Lisa of Twin Cities Frugal Mom, writing up two days in Medora with her husband and teenagers, part of a six-day North Dakota road trip and now a full family guide to the town.

Her guide covers a lot of ground. Wild horses, bison and prairie dogs along the South Unit scenic drive. The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library, where visitors are onboarded at the entrance and given a wristband that unlocks interactive stops through the galleries, including a campaign poster you build yourself, and where the Amazon expedition plays out in an immersive theater. Steak cooked fondue-style at Pitchfork Steak Fondue, then a few steps to the Medora Musical and a ride down the outdoor escalator into the amphitheater, with live horses and fireworks in the show. The North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame. The Harold Schafer Heritage Center, which costs nothing. Medora's new free trolley, which she recommends for anyone staying in town.

And huckleberry ice cream, which she says is worth seeking out.

Her answer to whether Medora is worth visiting runs one word: "Absolutely." Her advice is to give it at least two days.

Thank you, Twin Cities Frugal Mom, for bringing the family west and writing it all down.

#OTD in 1884, Theodore Roosevelt sat down in Dakota Territory to write his friend Henry Cabot Lodge, and spent most of the letter on politics before getting to the part he clearly enjoyed:

"In a day or two I start out, with two hunters, six riding ponies and a canvas topped 'prairie schooner' for the Bighorn Mountains. You would be amused to see me, in my broad sombrero hat, fringed and beaded buckskin shirt, horse hide chaparajos or riding trousers, and cowhide boots, with braided bridle and silver spurs."

He was 25. Six months earlier, on a single February day, his mother and his wife had died in the same house — Mittie of typhoid before dawn, Alice eleven hours later, two days after giving birth. He wrote one line in his diary, under a large black X: "The light has gone out of my life." Then he went west.

The buckskin suit was not something he found. He had it made — ordered from a Badlands woman named Mrs. Maddox, who measured him at her cabin. Roosevelt wanted to look like the thing he was trying to become, and he was clear-eyed about the theatre of it: "You would be amused to see me."

The rest of the letter is a young man arguing about his party. He tells Lodge he cannot call Blaine and Logan "fit nominees, or proper persons to fill the offices of President and Vice President," and that he may skip election day entirely: "indeed I may be in Dakotah on election day."

He also takes a shot at the Anglophile hunting set, whose American drag hunts chased an anise-soaked bag rather than a live fox. Roosevelt preferred "that description of sport which needs a buckskin shirt to that whose votaries adopt the red coat." Then, unimprovably: "A buffalo is nobler game than an anise seed bag."

He headed the letter Little Missouri, Dakotah — the rough town on the west bank, across the river from Medora.

#OTD in 1891, Ethel Carow Roosevelt was born at Sagamore Hill — Theodore's fourth child, and Edith's third.

She is the Roosevelt child most people cannot name. Alice was famous. Ted, Kermit, Archie and Quentin all went to war; Quentin did not come home, and Archie came home badly wounded. Ethel gets left out of the story, which is a shame, because she may have been the most quietly formidable of them.

On September 26, 1914 — weeks after Europe went to war, and years before America did — Ethel sailed for France with her husband, the surgeon Richard Derby. He operated at the American Ambulance Hospital at Neuilly-sur-Seine, outside Paris. She nursed there.

She was 23. She left a five-month-old son at Sagamore Hill with her parents, and was the first of Roosevelt's six children to go to the war that would eventually take the youngest of them.

Then she came home and did the unglamorous thing for the next sixty years.

Her father died in 1919. Quentin was already dead in France. Kermit died in Alaska in 1943, Ted in Normandy in 1944. Edith died in 1948. A few minutes before midnight on August 13, 1906, shots were fired in the streets of Brownsville, Texas. A bartender named Frank Natus was killed. A police lieutenant lost an arm. By the town's own count, roughly 200 rounds in about ten minutes.

The town blamed the soldiers of the 25th Infantry — three all-Black companies at Fort Brown, arrived barely two weeks earlier. In those weeks the men had been refused service in bars, shoved off sidewalks, beaten, and warned their brains might be blown out.

Their white commander, Major Charles Penrose, had put them under curfew that night. When the shooting started, the call to arms found every soldier present or accounted for.

Not one man would name a culprit. The Army read that silence as conspiracy. The evidence was spent shell casings, produced the next morning by the town — found in a tight circle a foot across, a pattern no fired rifle makes.

The commander of the Army's Southwestern Division cabled Washington plainly: "CITIZENS OF BROWNSVILLE ENTERTAIN RACE HATRED TO AN EXTREME DEGREE … PROVOCATION GIVEN THE SOLDIERS NOT TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT."

Roosevelt discharged 167 men without honor. No trial was held. Among them were career soldiers with service reaching back to the Indian Wars and Cuba — including First Sergeant Mingo Sanders, who remembered sharing hardtack with Colonel Roosevelt after Las Guasimas.

The order was dated November 5, 1906. It was held thirty-six hours, until after Election Day. Black voters had already gone to the polls.

Roosevelt never reconsidered: "The order in question will in no way be rescinded or modified."

In 1972 the Army reversed every discharge and called it a gross injustice. One man lived to see it: Dorsie Willis, who got his honorable discharge in a Minneapolis church on his eighty-seventh birthday, and $25,000 from Congress the year after — sixty-eight years late.

#OTD in 1914, a Panama Railroad steamer called the Ancon carried a few hundred officials and a hold of freight from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the Panama Canal was open.

It was meant to be far more than that. More than a hundred warships were to gather at Hampton Roads, pass through the canal in procession and sail on to the world's fair at San Francisco, with President Wilson aboard the old battleship Oregon at the head of the line.

None of it happened. Eleven days before the Ancon's transit, Germany had marched into Belgium. The fleets were needed elsewhere, and all but the most modest ceremony was quietly dropped. The Ancon made the run from Colón to Balboa in about nine hours, and the world barely looked up.

Theodore Roosevelt, who had done more than anyone to make that morning possible, was not there. He had been out of office five years. He and Edith spent the day on Long Island at a wedding — his old Chief Forester, Gifford Pinchot, marrying Cornelia Bryce at her parents' house in Roslyn.

There is something fitting in it. The canal was the most physically enormous thing Roosevelt ever set in motion, and it opened without him, on a day the world was too busy to notice, while he stood in a garden watching a friend get married.

How he got it built is still argued over. In 1903 the United States backed a revolution that separated Panama from Colombia, recognized the new republic within three days, and had a signed treaty for the canal zone inside three weeks. Colombia never accepted it; in 1921 the United States paid it $25 million. Roosevelt's own summary, delivered in a speech in 1911, was "I took the Isthmus."

Both things are true at once: the canal changed world trade permanently, and the manner of its getting is still contested more than a century later.

Amanda came out from @JLGArchitects last week with Ellie, her French bulldog. Ellie gets around in a wheelchair.

They started at the rocking chairs from the parking lot. Then they just… kept going. Down the boardwalk, up onto the green roof, all the way across. Every foot of it. Ellie's wheels never met a single step.

That is not luck. The mile-long boardwalk loop that climbs over the Library's 121,000-square-foot living roof was drawn to be traveled by everyone — no stairs, no workaround, no separate route for anyone who needs one. @Snohetta designed it that way from the beginning, and JLG Architects, as architect of record, saw it built that way.

The Badlands worked on T.R. because he could get out into them. A building set at their edge ought to give everybody that same chance.

Leashed pets are welcome on the grounds — boardwalk and roof included. Bring yours.

#OTD in 1884, Theodore Roosevelt made a list.

He was about to ride from the Little Missouri to the Bighorn Mountains — two months overland, most of it through country nobody had mapped for him. So he wrote down what he was taking.

A light "prairie schooner" with a canvas cover, pulled by two stout horses. Four riding ponies, each described by temperament: "Blackie, a stout, swift rather vicious pony; Splitear, very enduring; Brownie, willing and swift, but very nervous; and Roachie, quiet and rather small."

Then the clothes. A buckskin suit, sealskin chaparajos, a coonskin overcoat, an otter fur robe to sleep in — "buttoning into a bag form" — an oilskin slicker, boots and moccasins, a sombrero, overalls, a jersey, two flannel shirts, three suits of light underclothing and three of heavy, heavy socks, "plenty of handkerchiefs," soap, towels.

Then the food: flour, bacon, beans, coffee, sugar, salt. And, in the same breath, "a little brandy and cholera mixture."

Then this: "My battery consists of long 45 colt revolver, 150 cartridges; no 10 choke bore, 300 cartridges, shotgun; a 45-75 Winchester repeater, with 1000 cartridges; a 40-90 Sharps, 150 cartridges; a 50-150 double barreled Webly express, 100 cartridges."

Five guns. Exactly 1,700 rounds.

He was 25. He had first come to Dakota Territory in September 1883, and had been ranching there ever since. He went with his foreman, Bill Merrifield, and a teamster named Norman Lebo — an Ohio blacksmith and Union veteran — who drove the wagon and cooked.

The trip proper began two days later. Writing to his sister Bamie the day before he left, he mentioned in passing that on the day he made this list, he had ridden 72 miles between dawn and darkness.

#OTD in 1879, a twenty-year-old Harvard student sat down on a Sunday at Oyster Bay and wrote one of the happiest things he ever put on paper.

"Every Sunday we have morning and evening prayers; I wish we could have them everyday.

"Motherling is just too sweet and pretty for anything; and I doubt if there ever were two more lovely and unselfish girls than dear, noble Bysie, and darling Little Pussie. These three, and my best friend, old brother Nell, give me as happy a home as a man could possibly have."

The family shorthand takes a moment to decode. Motherling is Mittie — Martha Bulloch Roosevelt, raised at Bulloch Hall, a slaveholding plantation in Roswell, Georgia, who told her children stories of the Old South. Bysie is Anna, the eldest, more often called Bamie, who became her brother's most trusted political adviser. Little Pussie is Corinne, the youngest, who became a poet. And old brother Nell is Elliott.

He had already lost his father, eighteen months before. What he did not know was how much more was coming.

Within five years, on a single February day in 1884, his mother and his young wife died in the same house. Elliott — the best friend, the brother he could do anything with — declined into alcoholism and died in 1894 at thirty-four, leaving a daughter named Eleanor.

Bamie and Corinne outlived him. He was twenty when he wrote this. That is rather the point of a happy Sunday: you don't know it's the good part.

#OTD in 1884, on the first day of the ride to the Bighorns, Theodore Roosevelt got caught in the open.

The diary entry is nine sentences long and there is not a wasted word in it:

"Made late start. Left wagon on prairie. Merrifield & I rode on and spent the night at Langs. Out in prairie got caught in driving hail storm; Sheltered in a washout. Wind so strong could hardly stand; ponies would not face it. Our 'slickers' and chaps kept us perfectly dry in spite of the driving rain. The Winchester 45-75 shoots beautifully."

That last sentence is the whole man. Hail hard enough that the horses refused to walk into it, wind he could barely stand up in, and the thing he wanted recorded for posterity was that the rifle worked well.

"Langs" is the ranch of Gregor Lang, a Scot who had come out to the Badlands to run cattle for a London financier. Roosevelt had headquartered at Lang's cabin during his first Badlands hunt the year before, and sat up talking with him until the small hours. Lang's teenage son Lincoln never got over it, and decades later he wrote one of the best first-hand accounts anyone has of what Roosevelt was actually like out there.

A washout, for anyone who hasn't stood in one, is a gully cut by runoff — a few feet of shelter in ground that offers none. Two men and two ponies, waiting out a hailstorm in a ditch.

It was day one.

#OTD in 1903, seven days after Colombia's senate voted unanimously to reject the canal treaty, Theodore Roosevelt sat down at Sagamore Hill and wrote to his Secretary of State.

"It seems that the great bulk of the best engineers are agreed that that route is the best; and I do not think that the Bogota lot of jack rabbits should be allowed permanently to bar one of the future highways of civilization."

He is talking about the elected legislature of a sovereign country.

The Hay–Herrán Treaty would have leased the United States a six-mile-wide canal zone across the Colombian province of Panama. Colombia's senate rejected it 24 to 0 — partly over money, and substantially over sovereignty. President Marroquín had seen it coming. A year earlier he had written privately that history would say either that he ruined Colombia by refusing the canal, or that he allowed it "scandalously injuring the rights of my country."

In private that month Roosevelt was cruder still, using an ethnic slur for Colombians.

Eleven weeks later Panama revolted. American warships and the American-run railroad kept Colombian troops from reaching the uprising, the United States recognized the new republic in three days, and a canal treaty was signed inside three weeks.

He never repented of it. But a decade on, in his autobiography, he allowed that Colombians had "many fine traits" and a cultivated class that "would reflect honor on the social life of any country" — a circle he set against what he called "the stagnation and illiteracy of the mass of the people" — before concluding that a nation must be judged by its government, and Colombia "had to take the consequences."

In 1921, two years after his death, the United States paid Colombia $25 million.

"It seems that the great bulk of the best engineers are agreed that that route is the best; and I do not think that the Bogota lot of jack rabbits should be allowed permanently to bar one of the future highways of civilization."

He is talking about the elected legislature of a sovereign country.

The Hay–Herrán Treaty would have leased the United States a six-mile-wide canal zone across the Colombian province of Panama. Colombia's senate rejected it 24 to 0 — partly over money, and substantially over sovereignty. President Marroquín had seen it coming. A year earlier he had written privately that history would say either that he ruined Colombia by refusing the canal, or that he allowed it "scandalously injuring the rights of my country."

In private that month Roosevelt was cruder still, using an ethnic slur for Colombians.

Eleven weeks later Panama revolted. American warships and the American-run railroad kept Colombian troops from reaching the uprising, the United States recognized the new republic in three days, and a canal treaty was signed inside three weeks.

He never repented of it. But a decade on, in his autobiography, he allowed that Colombians had "many fine traits" and a cultivated class that "would reflect honor on the social life of any country" — a circle he set against what he called "the stagnation and illiteracy of the mass of the people" — before concluding that a nation must be judged by its government, and Colombia "had to take the consequences."

In 1921, two years after his death, the United States paid Colombia $25 million.

#OTD in 1907, Theodore Roosevelt stood on a wooden platform at Provincetown, Massachusetts, laid the cornerstone of the Pilgrim Monument, and said the thing everyone still quotes — minus the sentence it sits in.

He had come by sea, on the yacht Mayflower. Most of the address is about the Puritans. Then it turns.

The market had been sliding all year. Roosevelt had spent that year prosecuting corporations, and plenty of people said the two were linked.

"During the present trouble with the stock market I have, of course, received countless requests and suggestions, public and private, that I should say or do something to ease the situation."

What he said is more careful than its reputation. Most of the trouble, he argued, was worldwide — Paris and Berlin were shaky too. But:

"...it may well be that the determination of the Government (in which, gentlemen, it will not waver), to punish certain malefactors of great wealth, has been responsible for something of the trouble; at least to the extent of having caused these men to combine to bring about as much financial stress as possible, in order to discredit the policy of the Government and thereby secure a reversal of that policy, so that they may enjoy unmolested the fruits of their own evil-doing."

Note what he is not claiming: not that his prosecutions broke the market, but that certain men were deliberately worsening the stress to force him to stop.

Two passages that rarely travel with it:

"In the man of great wealth who has earned his wealth honestly and uses it wisely we recognize a good citizen of the best type, worthy of all praise and respect."

"The rich man who with hard arrogance declines to consider the rights and the needs of those who are less well off, and the poor man who excites or indulges in envy and hatred of those who are better off, are alike alien to the spirit of our national life."

Two months later the Panic of 1907 arrived, and J. P. Morgan had to assemble a private rescue because there was no central bank. Congress created the Federal Reserve six years later.

Theodore Roosevelt wrote that in a letter on January 26, 1900 — and he was careful to say it wasn't his. He called it an old proverb he'd long been fond of. He just happened to be the man who made it famous.

This morning, that idea returns to the Badlands that shaped him.

More than 70,000 visitors have come to Medora in six weeks. Robbie Lauf explains why on The Flag.

70,000 visitors. Six weeks.

Executive Director Robbie Lauf sat down with Scott Hennen on The Flag this week, and the number he brought with him was not the one anyone projected. The Library was not expected to reach 70,000 guests until November. It got there in mid-August — averaging more than 10,000 people a week, running at roughly 90% capacity.

The license plates in the parking lot tell part of the story. A couple from Wales tells the rest. They flew in for two days, saw the Library, and flew home.

What are they finding when they get here? A sixth grader asking Theodore Roosevelt — in AI form — for advice about a disagreement with his sister, and getting an answer as thoughtful as the ones TR gives visitors who ask him about the Panama Canal. Grandparents at the photo stations, transformed into Rough Riders on Kettle Hill while the grandkids come apart laughing. And, past the doors, the Badlands themselves.

"It's about the Badlands," Lauf told Hennen. "It's about getting people outside."

The hope is that a few hours inside send visitors back out for a few more — into Theodore Roosevelt National Park, onto the Maah Daah Hey. That, Lauf said, is what TR would want: come to the museum, then get outside.

One request from Robbie: buy tickets before arriving. Entry is timed, and days are selling out.

#OTD in 1884, four days into a two-month ride from the Little Missouri to the Bighorns, Theodore Roosevelt woke to a sound he thought worth writing down.

"Frost in the night. Day clear, cool and windy; wheeling much better. Early in morning a great herd of 1500 beef steers passed us; they had been bedded near us, and all night we had heard the cowboys singing and calling as they circled slowly round the herd."

"Wheeling" is the going underfoot for a wagon. The singing was working equipment. A startled cow runs, and a running cow takes fifteen hundred others with her, so night riders circled the bedground keeping up a steady human noise — so the cattle always knew where the men were and nothing arrived as a surprise.

Then the entry turns.

"Our dog, a greyhound, died from wolf poison. We made about 25 miles through broken prairie; are camped by what I suppose to be the head waters of O'Fallon Creek. Saw no living game; but hundreds of buffalo skulls and old carcasses."

Read those sentences together and you have the northern plains in August 1884. Fifteen hundred cattle where the buffalo had been. Wolf poison in that country almost always meant strychnine, put out in baits and carcasses, killing whatever found it first. And bones — hundreds of them — from a slaughter that had finished a year or two before he rode through.

He was twenty-five. He had come out in 1883 to shoot a buffalo and very nearly failed to find one. He would spend his presidency putting roughly 230 million acres under federal protection.

He had also, by this point, been sleeping on the ground beside two men long enough to size them up:

"Lebo is a chatty, tough old plainsman, full of expedients, and ready with the wits and hands. Merrifield is a good looking fellow, who shoots and rides beautifully; a reckless, self-confident man."

Norman Lebo drove the wagon and cooked. Bill Merrifield was his ranch foreman. The creek he guessed at heads in what is now southeastern Montana. If he had it right, somewhere in those four days they had crossed out of Dakota.

#OTD in 1902, Theodore Roosevelt climbed into an electric car in Hartford, Connecticut, and rode through the city for nearly three hours.

Look at the photograph. Police flank the car on bicycles — then about the most advanced personal transport a city could offer. Mounted men ride ahead and alongside. In the middle is a Columbia Electric Victoria Phaeton, built in Hartford, the President in the front seat, Colonel Jacob Lyman Greene beside him in a top hat, two liveried attendants perched high at the back exactly where they would have sat on a carriage. Top speed thirteen miles an hour.

Three generations of getting around, in one frame, at the same pace.

Now a correction, because a presidential library ought to make it. You will read in many places — including books on this Library's own shelves — that Roosevelt was the first president to ride in an automobile. He was not. William McKinley was. F. O. Stanley gave him a ride in a Stanley Steamer and McKinley did not care for it: eighteen miles an hour struck him as too fast, he never rode in one again, and he is said to have told a friend that Stanley was too optimistic to think such machines would replace the horse. Accounts differ on exactly when. Within months McKinley was dead and Roosevelt had his job.

Hartford was a different first, and a more consequential one: a sitting president riding in an automobile in public, as part of the work, with an escort around him. The first presidential motorcade.

There is a hard coda. Twelve days later, on the last morning of the same tour, Roosevelt's horse-drawn barouche was struck by a speeding trolley outside Pittsfield, Massachusetts. He was thrown into the road, cut about the face, with a blow to the left leg that turned septic three weeks later and put him in an Indianapolis hospital for surgery. William Craig, the Secret Service man riding with him, went under the wheels — the first Secret Service agent to die in the line of duty. The motorman pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was sentenced to six months and a $300 fine.

#OTD in 1883, a twenty-four-year-old New York assemblyman wrote to a retired naval commander to pin down some vacation dates, and let slip the sentence that explains the rest of his life.

"I am now being forced to make my plans in regard to the political campaign this Autumn, and so I am anxious to fix, as nearly as is convenient to you, what will be about the dates of our departure and return. I am fond of politics, but fonder still of a little big game hunting."

The commander was Henry Honychurch Gorringe, who in 1880 had brought Cleopatra's Needle — a granite obelisk some sixty-nine feet tall, weighing around 200 tons — from Alexandria to Central Park, then resigned his commission and went west. He bought a derelict Army cantonment in the Dakota Badlands, standing where the Northern Pacific crossed the Little Missouri, and set out to make it a hunting resort. Roosevelt wanted a buffalo before the last of them were gone. Gorringe had the country.

Then Gorringe pulled out. Late in August, without warning, days before the train left.

Roosevelt went anyway. Alice, his wife, was expecting their first child and wanted him to call it off — he had been ill, and he would now be going without a soul to travel with. He stepped off the train at Little Missouri, Dakota Territory, in the small hours of 8 September 1883, knowing nobody in it.

He found a guide the next morning — Joe Ferris, who was working as barn superintendent at Gorringe's cantonment and did not want the job, and who took one look at the spectacles and the grin and privately wrote the dude off. It rained. Roosevelt shot badly. He kept repeating, to Ferris's mounting exasperation, "It's dogged as does it."

He got his buffalo. Before he went home he had put money into a cattle outfit on the Little Missouri, the Maltese Cross. Ferris's verdict by then: "a plumb good sort."

Everything downstream of that — the Elkhorn, the killing winter of 1886–87, the conservation presidency, this Library standing in Medora — runs back through a letter about scheduling a hunting trip.

#OTD in 1884, about a hundred miles from any house, Theodore Roosevelt turned a water keg on its end, used it as a desk, and wrote two letters. Then he handed them to a stranger on horseback and hoped for the best.

He was a week out from the Little Missouri on a seven-week ride to the Bighorns. To his sister Bamie:

"I am writing this on an upturned water-keg, by our canvas-covered wagon, while the men are making tea, and the solemn old ponies are grazing round about me. I am going to trust it to the tender mercies of a stray cowboy whom we have just met, and who may or may not post it when he gets to 'Powderville,' a delectable log hamlet some seventy miles north of us."

The second letter went to Henry Cabot Lodge, who was in the middle of a hard fight for a seat in Congress — a race he would lose that November. It opens with an apology for the stationery and then gets to the real problem:

"...whether this letter is, or is not, ever delivered depends partly on Providence, and partly on the good-will of an equally inscrutable personage, either a cowboy or a horse-thief, whom we have just met, and who has volunteered to post it — my men are watching him with anything but friendly eyes, as they think he is going to try to steal our ponies. (To guard against this possibility he is to sleep between my foreman and myself — delectable bedfellow he'll prove, doubtless.)"

That is the arrangement. The only postal service for a hundred miles in any direction is a man his own crew expects to rob them, so they put him in the middle of the bed.

Roosevelt had no particular news. He wrote because he wanted to talk politics with a friend and there was nobody to talk to:

"I heartily enjoy this life, with its perfect freedom, for I am very fond of hunting, and there are few sensations I prefer to that of galloping over these rolling, limitless prairies, rifle in hand."

Both letters arrived.

#OTD in 1905, in the middle of a storm on Long Island Sound, Theodore Roosevelt went to the bottom of the sea.

The USS Plunger was the Navy's first purpose-built submarine — the Holland, bought in 1900, had been built on speculation. Sixty-four feet, one torpedo tube, a gasoline engine that filled the hull with fumes. She had been towed to Oyster Bay behind a tug to run trials near Sagamore Hill. On the afternoon of 25 August, with rain coming down hard and the swells rolling in, the President came aboard, went down the hatch, and spent the better part of an hour submerged.

He did not simply ride. He took the helm, started the electric motor, and worked the levers that flooded the tanks. They rested on the bottom. They ran a torpedo drill. They shut off every light to see what losing power would feel like.

Why a sitting president climbed into an experimental boat in a gale is the interesting part, and he answered it himself in a letter written twelve days later:

"I went down in it chiefly because I did not like to have the officers and enlisted men think I wanted them to try things I was reluctant to try myself."

He added, with characteristic balance, that he believed "a good deal can be done with these submarines, although there is always the danger of people getting carried away with the idea and thinking that they can be of more use than they possibly could be."

He told another correspondent that he had never in his life had "such a diverting day . . . nor so much enjoyment in so few hours."

The Navy at that time classed submarine service as shore duty and paid it accordingly. Roosevelt, having spent an afternoon inside one, disagreed, and ordered that submariners receive extra pay for any day their boat went under. He signed the order that November. That is where American submarine pay begins.

He did all of this in the same week he was brokering the end of the Russo-Japanese War. The treaty was signed at Portsmouth eleven days later, and it won him the Nobel Peace Prize.

Why a sitting president climbed into an experimental boat in a gale is the interesting part, and he answered it himself in a letter written twelve days later:

"I went down in it chiefly because I did not like to have the officers and enlisted men think I wanted them to try things I was reluctant to try myself."

He added, with characteristic balance, that he believed "a good deal can be done with these submarines, although there is always the danger of people getting carried away with the idea and thinking that they can be of more use than they possibly could be."

He told another correspondent that he had never in his life had "such a diverting day . . . nor so much enjoyment in so few hours."

The Navy at that time classed submarine service as shore duty and paid it accordingly. Roosevelt, having spent an afternoon inside one, disagreed, and ordered that submariners receive extra pay for any day their boat went under. He signed the order that November. #OTD in 1885, a grand jury in Mandan indicted the Marquis de Morès for murder in the first degree.

The Marquis founded Medora and named it for his wife. He had been involved in the killing of Riley Luffsey in 1883 and had twice seen charges dismissed. This time it went forward.

Roosevelt had fallen out with him that summer over cattle, having driven a herd to the Marquis's slaughterhouse at an agreed six cents a pound; at delivery the Marquis said Chicago had dropped. A. T. Packard, who edited the local paper, was there:

"Did you agree to pay six cents for these cattle?"

"Yes. But the Chicago price —"

"Are you going to pay six cents for them?"

"No; I will pay five and a half cents."

Roosevelt turned to his cowpunchers. "Drive 'em out, boys," he said. Packard added there was no particular ill feeling in it: Roosevelt credited the Marquis with honestly believing the market ought to count.

Eight days later the Marquis wrote to Roosevelt from his cell, convinced that Joe Ferris — Roosevelt's friend and first Badlands guide — had helped build the case:

"I thought you my friend. If you are my enemy I want to know it. I am always on hand as you know, and between gentlemen it is easy to settle matters of that sort directly."

Roosevelt read that as a challenge. He asked Bill Sewall to be his second and said that, having the choice, he would take rifles at twelve paces. He wrote back:

"Most emphatically I am not your enemy; if I were you would know it, for I would be an open one, and would not have asked you to my house nor gone to yours. As your final words, however, seem to imply a threat it is due to myself to say that the statement is not made through any fear of possible consequences to me; I too, as you know, am always on hand, and ever ready to hold myself accountable in any way for anything I have said or done."

No duel. He was acquitted that September. Roosevelt was twenty-six.

He left the Badlands the next year. In France he became one of the era's leading antisemitic agitators — the subject of Sergio Luzzatto's 2026 book The First Fascist.

#OTD in 1906, Theodore Roosevelt ordered the United States government to change how it spelled.

The instruction went to Charles A. Stillings, the Public Printer: every document coming out of the executive branch would adopt 300 respelled words drawn up by the Simplified Spelling Board, a body funded by Andrew Carnegie. Thru for through. Dropt for dropped. Kist for kissed.

Roosevelt thought he was doing something modest, and said so:

"It is not an attempt to do anything far-reaching or sudden or violent; or indeed anything very great at all. It is merely an attempt to cast what slight weight can properly be cast on the side of the popular forces which are endeavoring to make our spelling a little less foolish and fantastic."

His argument was that English spelling had always been in motion. Nobody, he pointed out, still wrote batte, sette, dimme, summe and fysshe, as the Elizabethans had. He was not inventing a change; he was declining to lag behind one.

The country disagreed, loudly. Newspapers mocked him for months. Congress was angrier still — and notably, the objection in Congress had less to do with spelling than with a president rewriting the language by executive order. In December the House resolved that its documents would use the spelling found in the dictionary. Roosevelt withdrew the order.

He was a good loser about it, in a letter that same month:

"I could not by fighting have kept the new spelling in, and it was evidently worse than useless to go into an undignified contest when I was beaten. Do you know that the one word as to which I thought the new spelling was wrong — thru — was more responsible than anything else for our discomfiture? But I am mighty glad I did the thing anyhow. In my own correspondence I shall continue using the new spelling."

He kept his word — simplified spellings turn up in his letters for years afterward.

#OTD in 1908, Theodore Roosevelt signed an order protecting a shallow alkali lake in Stutsman County, North Dakota. There were about fifty pelicans left on it.

American white pelicans had nested at Chase Lake in great numbers through the middle of the nineteenth century. By the turn of the century their numbers had fallen sharply, for a reason the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service still states plainly: people "made a regular practice of going to Chase Lake on Sunday afternoons to see how many pelicans they could kill."

The man who stopped it was not a president. H. H. McCumber came to the area in 1905, found only about 500 birds, watched the number keep falling, and petitioned the U.S. Biological Survey — the ancestor of today's Fish and Wildlife Service — to make the lake a refuge. By the time the order came, the count was down to fifty.

Roosevelt signed. Chase Lake became the fifteenth federal wildlife refuge in the country and the second of the two federal bird reservations he created in North Dakota, after Stump Lake in 1905. McCumber was made its first federal game warden.

When he left in 1918, he reported between 2,500 and 3,000 pelicans on the lake.

In 2000, a record 35,466 breeding pelicans were counted.

That is what the signature was for. A settler who could see what was happening, a government office that listened, and a president willing to sign — and a hundred and eighteen years later Chase Lake still holds one of the largest American white pelican nesting colonies in North America.

#OTD in 1884, Theodore Roosevelt made what he called the best shot he had ever made, paced out the distance to prove it, and kept the bullet.

It had been a miserable day. Up Clear Creek in what is now Wyoming, in country he called "very barren; broken, rolling, treeless, and covered with sage brush." Deep washouts across the road. The wagon stuck three times, and they had to help the team out with ropes hitched to the saddle trees of the riding horses. "Team nearly done out."

Then, in the afternoon:

"Roused three blacktail bucks; shot three times with Winchester at them running, going close but a little high, finally stopping them; two stood side by side; taking careful aim I broke the backs of both with one bullet; distance 431 paces (near 400 yards) actual walking. Best shot I ever made. Kept bullet."

Two deer with one bullet, at a distance he put at close to four hundred yards. It is his own account, in his own diary, and it is the only account we have.

The detail that gives it away is "actual walking." He did not estimate the range. He walked it, counting — 431 paces — because he wanted the number to be right. He knew his own limits. Four years earlier, hunting with his brother Elliott, he had written flatly in the same diary: "Elliott is a good shot; I am not. But I am improving steadily."

So he kept the bullet. Somewhere in the accounting of a life that would include a war, a presidency and a Nobel Prize, a twenty-five-year-old put a piece of lead in his pocket because he wanted to remember.

#OTD in 1897, Assistant Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt mailed the President of the United States a pamphlet, and quietly told on his own boss in the covering note.

He had spent his "spare hours" that summer assembling every passage he could find in which a previous president had argued for a stronger navy. Washington, Jackson, Lincoln, Grant. Read back to back it struck him as a powerful piece of propaganda, so he decided to publish it. Thomas Jefferson did not make the cut.

Protocol required showing it to his actual superior first. Secretary of the Navy John D. Long — who was already tired of his deputy's loud enthusiasm for battleships — approved it on one condition: that Roosevelt insert the words "in my own opinion" into the introduction, so nobody mistook it for department policy.

Roosevelt agreed, in writing, with every appearance of humility: "Hereafter I shall adopt exactly the rule you suggest about my official publications, and about my general utterances also."

Then he sent an advance copy to President McKinley with a note pointing out this:

"On the first page, where I speak of the need of strengthening the Navy, the words 'in my own opinion,' were put in at the suggestion of the Secretary."

Which is to say: the hedge you are about to read is not mine. It is the Secretary's.

It appeared that year in the Proceedings of the United States Naval Institute, and the Government Printing Office issued it as a pamphlet in September: The Naval Policy of America as Outlined in Messages of the Presidents of the United States from the Beginning to the Present Day. By Edmund Morris's account it drew admiring notice, "timely" being the adjective most often used. Eight months later the United States was at war with Spain, and within weeks the man who compiled it had resigned to go and fight in it.

#OTD in 1897, Assistant Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt mailed the President of the United States a pamphlet, and quietly told on his own boss in the covering note.

He had spent his "spare hours" that summer assembling every passage he could find in which a previous president had argued for a stronger navy. Washington, Jackson, Lincoln, Grant. Read back to back it struck him as a powerful piece of propaganda, so he decided to publish it. Thomas Jefferson did not make the cut.

Protocol required showing it to his actual superior first. Secretary of the Navy John D. Long — who was already tired of his deputy's loud enthusiasm for battleships — approved it on one condition: that Roosevelt insert the words "in my own opinion" into the introduction, so nobody mistook it for department policy.

Roosevelt agreed, in writing, with every appearance of humility: "Hereafter I shall adopt exactly the rule you suggest about my official publications, and about my general utterances also."

Then he sent an advance copy to President McKinley with a note pointing out this:

"On the first page, where I speak of the need of strengthening the Navy, the words 'in my own opinion,' were put in at the suggestion of the Secretary."

Which is to say: the hedge you are about to read is not mine. It is the Secretary's.

It appeared that year in the Proceedings of the United States Naval Institute, and the Government Printing Office issued it as a pamphlet in September: The Naval Policy of America as Outlined in Messages of the Presidents of the United States from the Beginning to the Present Day. By Edmund Morris's account it drew admiring notice, "timely" being the adjective most often used. Eight months later the United States was at war with Spain, and within weeks the man who compiled it had resigned to go and fight in it.

#OTD in 1910, out of office nearly eighteen months, Theodore Roosevelt spoke to 30,000 people at Osawatomie, Kansas, at the dedication of a park honoring John Brown. Grand Army veterans were in the crowd and he spoke straight at them, quoting Lincoln. What he set out became the manifesto of the Republican insurgency.

By any measure of 1910 it was radical: federal supervision of every corporation doing interstate business, a graduated income tax, an inheritance tax on big fortunes, workmen's compensation, child labor limits. He did not pretend it was small:

"This, I know, implies a policy of a far more active governmental interference with social and economic conditions in this country than we have yet had, but I think we have got to face the fact that such an increase in governmental control is now necessary."

Then he turned on the reformers:

"If I could ask but one thing of my fellow countrymen, my request would be that, whenever they go in for reform, they remember the two sides, and that they always exact justice from one side as much as from the other. I have small use for the public servant who can always see and denounce the corruption of the capitalist, but who cannot persuade himself, especially before election, to say a word about lawless mob-violence. And I have equally small use for the man, be he a judge on the bench or editor of a great paper, or wealthy and influential private citizen, who can see clearly enough and denounce the lawlessness of mob-violence, but whose eyes are closed so that he is blind when the question is one of corruption of business on a gigantic scale."

He knew how he was being read:

"Here in Kansas there is one paper which habitually denounces me as the tool of Wall Street, and at the same time frantically repudiates the statement that I am a Socialist on the ground that that is an unwarranted slander of the Socialists."

The country divided. Some called it socialistic; others, among the greatest speeches ever delivered. Two years later it was the platform he ran on against the man he had put in the White House.

#OTD in 1878, a nineteen-year-old about to start his junior year at Harvard sat down and admitted he had no idea what to do with his life.

"I had a long talk with Uncle Jim about my future life; I have absolutely no idea what I shall do when I leave college."

His father had been dead nearly seven months. Theodore Roosevelt Sr. — the man his son called the best he ever knew — had died in February at forty-six of a malignant tumor of the bowel, after months in which the family watched and could do nothing. The son had not been there at the end.

The next line of the diary is not a plan. It is grief:

"Oh, Father, my Father, no words can tell how I shall miss your counsel and advice!"

And then, immediately, the only thing he can think of to do about it:

"However, for the next two years my duty is clear—to study well and live like a brave Christian gentleman."

That is the whole entry. A boy with no direction, no father, and one rule he has decided to follow until something better arrives.

Uncle Jim was James Alfred Roosevelt, his father's brother, a New York banker, and now the man with the final say over the family's money.

Worth remembering what happens next, and how little of it he could see coming. Within six years he would be a published historian, a state assemblyman, a widower and a rancher. Twenty-three years later he would be president. On this day in 1878 the plan was to study well and behave decently, and that was all of it.

A hundred and twenty-five years ago today, at the Minnesota State Fair, Vice President Theodore Roosevelt quoted the line he is still quoted for.

"A good many of you are probably acquainted with the old proverb: 'Speak softly and carry a big stick—you will go far.'"

Three things about it are not what people assume.

The first is that he had been using it for more than a year and a half, and not about foreign policy. He wrote it down in January 1900, in a letter to Henry Sprague, in a good mood after forcing the New York Republican machine to drop a corrupt state insurance superintendent: "I have always been fond of the West African proverb." The most famous line in the history of American foreign policy started life as a comment on a patronage fight in Albany.

The second is that nobody has found the proverb. No earlier use of it has ever turned up, and Roosevelt never said where he had heard it.

The third is the part that gets left off. The line is not a boast, and the rest of the same paragraph says so:

"If a man continually blusters, if he lacks civility, a big stick will not save him from trouble; and neither will speaking softly avail, if back of the softness there does not lie strength, power. In private life there are few beings more obnoxious than the man who is always loudly boasting; and if the boaster is not prepared to back up his words his position becomes absolutely contemptible. So it is with the nation. It is both foolish and undignified to indulge in undue self-glorification, and, above all, in loose-tongued denunciation of other peoples."

The big stick without the soft speech, in other words, is just a man shouting.

The speech is called "National Duties," and the rest of it is harder going: a defense of American rule in the Philippines in the language of civilization and barbarism, and of the taking of Dakota from the people who lived there. Both things are in the same address.

Twelve days later William McKinley was dead and Roosevelt was President of the United States.

#OTD in 1902, on the last morning of a New England tour, a streetcar ran into the President of the United States.

Roosevelt was in an open carriage outside Pittsfield, Massachusetts, with Governor Winthrop Murray Crane and his secretary George Cortelyou. An electric trolley came down the hill fast. William Craig, the Secret Service man riding with them, saw it coming and shouted.

The car struck the carriage. Roosevelt was thrown into the road. Cortelyou was concussed. Craig went under the wheels and was killed — the first Secret Service agent to die in the line of duty.

He was a Scot from Glasgow, six foot four, a champion broadswordsman who had spent twelve years in the Royal Horse Guards, some of it guarding Queen Victoria. He had been assigned to Roosevelt in Buffalo almost exactly a year earlier — days after standing on McKinley's detail the afternoon McKinley was shot.

Roosevelt got up, found his spectacles unbroken in the grass, and told the doctor to see to the others. Then he saw what was under the trolley. He went at the motorman with his fists up, and men had to get between them. Then he came back and knelt by the wheels.

"Poor Craig," he said. "How my children will feel."

He kept the rest of the day's stops but made no speeches. By evening he was on the presidential yacht, headed home.

The injury that mattered turned out not to be the face. A blow to his left leg abscessed over the following three weeks and needed emergency surgery in Indianapolis, which put him on crutches and cut short a second speaking trip. He had trouble with that leg for the rest of his life.

The motorman, Euclid Madden, pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was sentenced to six months in jail and a $300 fine.

Of Craig, Roosevelt said: "The man who was killed was one of whom I was fond and whom I greatly prized for his loyalty and faithfulness." Craig had been closest of all to four-year-old Quentin. They used to read the funny papers together.

#OTD in 1879, a twenty-year-old Theodore Roosevelt spent the day packing a canoe, and wrote down exactly what went in it.

"Spent the day preparing for my Munsungun trip; I shall go in a canoe, alone with Seawall. For provisions I took pork and hardtack & some flour; we have a shelter tent, two blankets & some cooking utensils; & one complete change of clothing each. I take 50 cartridges for the rifle and 100 for the shotgun. I shall only use moccasins."

Pork, hardtack, flour. A shelter tent. Two blankets. One change of clothes. A hundred and fifty rounds. No boots.

"Seawall" is Bill Sewall — William Wingate Sewall, a Maine guide thirteen years his senior who had been taking this asthmatic, nearsighted college boy into the woods and finding, to his own surprise, that he could keep up. Sewall's first impression, set down years later, was of "a thin, pale youngster with bad eyes and a weak heart."

They went up to Munsungan Lake, the two of them, and camped.

Five years later Roosevelt wrote to Sewall from Dakota Territory and asked him to come out and run a cattle ranch with him. Sewall had never seen the Badlands and did not want to go. He went anyway, with his nephew Wilmot Dow; the families followed, and Sewall's son was born at the Elkhorn. For two years they ran it. In 1886 Sewall and Dow were two of the three men who went down the ice-choked Little Missouri after the thieves who stole Roosevelt's boat.

He outlived him by eleven years. Around 1921, two years after Roosevelt died, Sewall walked back in to the shore of Munsungan Lake with Game Warden Walter Wood and a man named Russell Whitman, cut a blaze into a pine and built a cairn of stones at the foot of it, to mark the place where the two of them had camped. Somebody photographed it. The old man in the suspenders, leaning on the tree and watching the younger men stack the rocks, is Bill Sewall.

For provisions I took pork and hardtack & some flour; we have a shelter tent, two blankets & some cooking utensils; & one complete change of clothing each. I take 50 cartridges for the rifle and 100 for the shotgun. I shall only use moccasins."

Pork, hardtack, flour. A shelter tent. Two blankets. One change of clothes. A hundred and fifty rounds. No boots.

"Seawall" is Bill Sewall — William Wingate Sewall, a Maine guide thirteen years his senior who had been taking this asthmatic, nearsighted college boy into the woods and finding, to his own surprise, that he could keep up. Sewall's first impression, set down years later, was of "a thin, pale youngster with bad eyes and a weak heart."

They went up to Munsungan Lake, the two of them, and camped.

Five years later Roosevelt wrote to Sewall from Dakota Territory and asked him to come out and run a cattle ranch with him. Sewall had never seen the Badlands and did not want to go. He went anyway, with his nephew Wilmot Dow; the families followed, and Sewall's son was born at the Elkhorn. For two years they ran it. In 1886 Sewall and Dow were two of the three men who went down the ice-choked Little Missouri after the thieves who stole Roosevelt's boat.

He outlived him by eleven years. Around 1921, two years after Roosevelt died, Sewall walked back in to the shore of Munsungan Lake with Game Warden Walter Wood and a man named Russell Whitman, cut a blaze into a pine and built a cairn of stones at the foot of it, to mark the place where the two of them had camped. Somebody photographed it. The old man in the suspenders, leaning on the tree and watching the younger men stack the rocks, is Bill Sewall.

#OTD in 1905, at 3:47 in the afternoon, Russia and Japan signed a peace treaty in a shipyard building at Kittery, Maine. The Russo-Japanese War was over. The man who had spent the summer forcing it to happen was two hundred miles away and never once set foot in the room.

Theodore Roosevelt ran the Portsmouth conference from Sagamore Hill, his house at Oyster Bay — largely by going around the diplomats. He wrote to General Francis V. Greene the same day the treaty was signed:

"…only by disregarding the old conventional diplomatic methods… I communicated personally with the Czar, the Mikado, the Kaiser, Balfour, Rouvier, and so forth."

A month earlier he had put both delegations aboard the presidential yacht Mayflower off Oyster Bay and fed them a standing buffet — no seating plan, no head of the table — so that no one held the place of honor. Then he solved the impossible question of whose sovereign to toast first:

"Gentlemen: I propose a toast to which there will be no answer, and which I ask you to drink in silence, standing. I drink to the welfare and prosperity of the sovereigns and peoples of the two great nations whose representatives have met one another on this ship."

Japan gave up its claim to an indemnity. Russia gave up the southern half of Sakhalin. Four plenipotentiaries signed — Baron Komura Jutarō and Takahira Kogorō for Japan, Sergei Witte and Baron Roman Rosen for Russia — four copies, two in English and two in French. Witte was made a count on his return; the treaty was the reason.

In Tokyo, police blocked a protest rally at Hibiya Park against a peace many Japanese considered a humiliation. The city rioted. At least eleven people were killed and more than a thousand injured, and martial law was declared the next morning.

The following year Roosevelt became the first American to win a Nobel Prize in any category. He did not go to Norway for it — the American minister accepted on his behalf — and he did not deliver his Nobel lecture until 1910, more than a year after leaving office.

#OTD in 1901, at seven minutes past four in the afternoon, President William McKinley stood in the Temple of Music at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, shaking hands with anyone who cared to shake his.

His secretary, George Cortelyou, had struck the reception from the schedule twice. Twice McKinley put it back.

It was hot, and the line was full of handkerchiefs. The man who reached the front had one wrapped around his right hand. He knocked the President's hand aside and fired twice at arm's length. One bullet struck the breastbone and fell out of McKinley's clothing when he was undressed for surgery. The other passed through both walls of the stomach and was never found.

McKinley's first words were about his wife. His next, as the earliest accounts have them, were about the man on the floor being beaten by soldiers and detectives: "Let no one hurt him."

The ambulance took eleven minutes. The operating room had no electric light rigged when they began — at a fair lit by Niagara Falls — so two physicians held light on the wound while the surgeon worked. Two X-ray machines were within reach, one on exhibit at the Exposition and one rushed from Edison's laboratory. Neither was used.

For six days the bulletins were good. On the morning of 12 September: "He has taken a little solid food and relished it." Eleven hours later: "not quite so favorable." By the small hours of the 13th: "the gravest apprehension." He died at 2:15 on the morning of 14 September.

—

Standing directly behind the assassin in that line was James Parker, a Black waiter at an Exposition restaurant. Secret Service agent Samuel Ireland, who had been standing in front of the President, told the Buffalo Courier the next morning that Parker struck the man in the neck, reached for the revolver, and knocked it from his hand before a third shot could be fired.

Ireland was never called at the trial. The agent who was called, George Foster, testified: "I never saw no colored man in the whole fracas." Parker's name appears exactly once in the entire transcript, and not from a witness — from defense counsel, asking. Another Black employee of the Temple of Music, who stood eight feet away, did testify, and was never asked about him.

Parker turned down the men who wanted to exhibit him. "I happened to be in a position where I could aid in the capture of the man," he told the Buffalo Commercial on 13 September. "I am no freak anyway. I do not want to be exhibited in all kinds of shows."

Vice President Theodore Roosevelt spent that afternoon on an island in Lake Champlain, at the Vermont Fish and Game League's outing, talking about a cougar hunt in Colorado. At half past five he was called to one of the few telephones on the island, where a Mrs. Butler, ringing from Burlington, told him there was a rumor the President had been shot.

#OTD in 1897, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy went to sea to watch battleships shoot at things. He brought an artist along.

Theodore Roosevelt joined the North Atlantic Squadron about thirty miles east of the Virginia capes, aboard the dispatch boat Dolphin. Rear Admiral Montgomery Sicard's ships were at sub-calibre practice; on learning that Roosevelt wanted to see the heavy guns, Sicard suspended it and designated the new battleship Iowa, commissioned that June, to fire her batteries in his presence. Most of her crew had never heard the main battery fired. A whaleboat was put out of service, some skylights broke, and a door or two came off its hinges.

The artist was Frederic Remington, whose drawings had done more than anyone's to fix in the American mind what a cowboy looked like. Roosevelt had been using him for a decade — Remington illustrated Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail in 1888 — and this time he wanted something else entirely. He wrote to him on 15 September:

"I wish I were with you out among the sage brush, the great brittle cottonwoods, and the sharply-channeled, barren buttes; but I am very glad at any rate to have had you along with the squadron; and I can't help looking upon you as an ally from henceforth on in trying to make the American people see the beauty and the majesty of our ships, and the heroic quality which lurks somewhere in all those who man and handle them."

To Henry Cabot Lodge he was simply happy: "Think of it, on the Atlantic Ocean, out of sight of land, going out to dinner to a battleship in evening dress without an overcoat!"

To Rudyard Kipling he reported that Remington "was very nearly blown up through incautiously getting too near the blast line of one of the 13-inch guns." Iowa's main battery was twelve-inch. The Assistant Secretary of the Navy got the caliber wrong.

Remington gave Harper's Weekly five drawings that year — a tug-of-war, winter at an army post, tarpon fishing, a wounded bull elk, and the horse show. Not one warship. Roosevelt was still nudging him in November: "we were all wishing that you would do something about the Navy some time." He never got his Navy pictures.

He got something else. Nine months later Remington was in Cuba with the army, and by the end of that year he had painted the charge of the Rough Riders. At Montauk that September, as the regiment prepared to muster out, Roosevelt's men presented him with a Remington bronze. He still had it fifteen years later: "Perhaps our most cherished possessions are a Remington bronze, 'The Bronco Buster,' given me by my men when the regiment was mustered out…"

#OTD in 1883, shortly after two in the morning, a twenty-four-year-old New York assemblyman stepped off a Northern Pacific train at Little Missouri, Dakota Territory, and stood in the dark.

Little Missouri was a handful of buildings on the west bank of the river. Medora, across the water, was five months old — the Marquis de Morès had founded it that April. The traveler hammered on the door of the Pyramid Park Hotel and dropped the name of Commander H. H. Gorringe, the retired naval officer who owned the old Army cantonment nearby, which was enough to end the argument. Upstairs was one long room with fourteen cots in it, known locally as the bull-pen. Thirteen were occupied. He paid two bits for the last one.

He had come to shoot a buffalo before there were none left to shoot, and he was nearly too late. The northern herd was in its last months; the final large herd on the northern plains would be destroyed that October, a few weeks after he arrived.

By morning he had a guide. He wrote to his wife Alice that same day about "a good looking hunter named Joe Ferris."

What followed was, by his own account, a fiasco — rain, wet blankets, biscuits gone soft, and bad shooting. "So far the trip had certainly not been a success," he wrote later, "although sufficiently varied as regards its incidents." Joe Ferris remembered a client who would not quit: "He could stand an awful lot of hard knocks, and he was always cheerful. You just couldn't knock him out of sorts." A neighbor, Lincoln Lang, put it less kindly: "He nearly killed poor Joe. He would not stop for anything."

He got his buffalo on 20 September. But the more consequential thing had happened two days earlier, on a log outside Gregor Lang's cabin, when he handed Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield a check for fourteen thousand dollars to go into the cattle business — more than his entire income for the year. Merrifield, decades later: "He handed us a check for fourteen thousand dollars, handed it right over to us on a verbal contract. He didn't have a scratch of a pen for it." Merrifield asked whether he wanted a receipt. "Oh, that's all right." A written contract followed nine days later, signed in St. Paul.

Twenty-seven years on, speaking at Fargo, he said it plainly: "I can never begin to say what I owe to North Dakota. It is not only that I never would have been president if it had not been for my experiences here in North Dakota…"

It started at two in the morning, in a fourteen-bunk room, with a man who had come to kill one animal.

#OTD in 1883, on his second day in Dakota Territory, Theodore Roosevelt rode about forty-five miles south down the Little Missouri to a cabin belonging to a man he had never met.

He had a horse now. The night before, at the Maltese Cross, he had tried to talk Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield out of a buckskin mare named Nell, failed, and bought her instead. Joe Ferris, telling it to Hermann Hagedorn more than thirty-five years later:

"By gosh, he wanted that saddle horse so bad that we were afraid to let him have it. Why, we didn't know him from Job's off ox. We didn't know but what he'd ride away with it. But, say, he wanted that horse so blamed bad, that when he see we weren't going to let him have it, he offered to buy it for cash."

Hagedorn called the mare Roosevelt's "first physical hold on the Bad Lands."

They started at dawn — Joe driving the buckboard, Roosevelt alongside on Nell — fording the river again and again as it wandered across their path, and reached the mouth of the Little Cannonball at sunset. Gregor Lang's cabin stood in a cluster of cottonwoods fifty yards from where the creek met the river.

Lang was a Scot. The London financier Sir John Pender had bought into a Little Missouri cattle company that spring and sent Lang out to keep an eye on it; by September Lang was running a ranch of his own on Pender's money. He had a sixteen-year-old son named Lincoln, who remembered the arrival for the rest of his life:

"Aided by the beam of light showing through the cabin door, I could make out that he was a young man, who wore large conspicuous-looking glasses, through which I was being regarded with interest by a pair of twinkling eyes. Amply supporting them was the expansive grin overspreading his prominent, forceful lower face, plainly revealing a set of larger white teeth. Smiling teeth, yet withal conveying a strong suggestion of hang-and-rattle. The kind of teeth that are made to hold anything they once close upon…"

Then Joe Ferris, who had just driven a buckboard forty-five miles, went to bed, and the New Yorker and the Scotsman sat up talking cattle until midnight.

Nine days later, on a log outside that cabin, Roosevelt handed Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield a check for fourteen thousand dollars.

#OTD in 1907, Theodore Roosevelt set aside 2,262,624 acres of Alaska rainforest — over the objection of his own Land Office.

Six months earlier Congress had taken the power away from him. An amendment to an agriculture bill forbade any new forest reserve, or any addition to one, in Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, Colorado or Wyoming "except by Act of Congress." In the two days before he signed that bill, Roosevelt signed thirty-two proclamations — twenty-one new reserves and eleven enlargements, about sixteen million acres — in those six states. Then he signed the bill.

The amendment did not name Alaska.

The Forest Service had wanted far more than it got. Inspector F. E. Olmsted recommended reserving essentially all of southeastern Alaska, and a map was drawn for a "Baranof National Forest." Richard Ballinger, Commissioner of the General Land Office, opposed creating any national forest in Alaska at all: the forests were not needed to protect a water supply, he argued, there was no fire hazard, and nothing needed replanting. His assistant commissioner, Fred Dennett, called the project a "conspiracy" to get around the ban on exporting Alaska timber. The map was withdrawn.

So W. A. Langille, the supervisor on the ground, drew a smaller one, and predicted: "The only objection to creation of the reserve will come from those who oppose the national forest policy on general principles."

He was wrong about that. Both Alaska territorial parties, Republican and Democratic, had adopted planks the year before demanding that the reserve already there be abolished.

Roosevelt signed anyway. Proclamation 772 set the land apart "for the use and benefit of the people." It states no acreage at all — every figure since has come from Land Office bookkeeping. Three weeks before he left office, on 16 February 1909, he added 8.7 million acres more.

The Tongass is now 16.7 million acres, the largest national forest in the country and the largest intact coastal temperate rainforest on earth. It is also Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian homeland, and the proclamations do not mention them. In 1959 the U.S. Court of Claims held that their aboriginal title had never been extinguished and that the proclamations creating the Tongass were an uncompensated taking. Damages were awarded in 1968 — though the court struck the award for fishing rights, which its own earlier opinion had called the most valuable thing they lost. Congress extinguished the remaining claims in 1971.

#OTD in 1900, the Republican candidate for vice president crossed eastern South Dakota by rail — Flandreau at eight in the morning, Madison at half past nine, Sioux Falls at midday, Vermillion at half past six, Yankton by torchlight in the evening. Eleven stops in a single day, two of them across the line in Iowa.

It had rained hard the night before. Theodore M. Knappen, a Minneapolis Journal staff correspondent travelling with the party, wrote up the Madison stop:

"At Madison the governor and company were hustled into carriages and driven to the opera house, a boys' band running along the sidewalks thumping out a tune. 'And this reminds me of old times,' said the governor to the newspaper men. 'I feel at home now. The wide muddy street, the high sidewalks, the straggling stores. How I would like to take a team and go out on the prairies after chickens for a whole day.'"

The mud was real. The Saint Paul Globe reported that "the rain of the preceding night had rendered the streets so muddy that an outdoor reception was impossible," so the local committee moved him into the opera house instead of the stand by the depot.

Roosevelt had ranched in Dakota Territory from 1883 to 1886 — up on the Little Missouri, in what by 1900 was North Dakota, a state away from the street he was standing on.

Not everyone was charmed. The Madison Daily Leader, a Populist paper, covered the visit on the eleventh and reported that when the carriage came up the street and went back down again there was not a single cheer: "it might as well have been an ice-wagon." On the twelfth it reprinted Knappen's dispatch under the headline "THE PRETTY STORY," explaining that it would "afford us a text or two for the future." On the thirteenth: "Mr. Roosevelt's tour is not a triumph but a vote-begging fizzle." The state's larger papers saw a different day — the Sioux Falls Argus-Leader headlined its account "Veni! Vidi! Vici!"

He kept going. The tally the newspapers printed on Election Day: 21,209 miles, 567 towns, 24 states, 673 speeches. Historians have since put the number of stops lower. One surviving day from an aide's timetable has seven speeches in it plus two solid hours of speaking after supper, with Sir Walter Scott and a book on birds wedged into the gaps.

He had told Mark Hanna at the outset how hard he could be worked: "I am as strong as a bull moose, and you can use me to the limit, taking heed of but one thing and that is my throat."

#OTD in 1906, from Sagamore Hill, Theodore Roosevelt finished a book he had not enjoyed and wrote to Henry Cabot Lodge about it.

The book was Winston Churchill's two-volume life of his father, Lord Randolph, published that January. Churchill was thirty-one and had sat in the House of Commons since 1901. Roosevelt was president.

"I have been over Winston Churchill's life of his father. I dislike the father and dislike the son, so I may be prejudiced. Still, I feel that, while the biographer and his subject possess some real farsightedness… yet they both possess or possessed such levity, lack of sobriety, lack of permanent principle, and inordinate thirst for that cheap form of admiration which is given to notoriety, as to make them poor public servants."

Lodge wrote back four days later, admitting he had not read the book: "The son I know; I have met him several times. He is undoubtedly clever but conceited to a degree which it is hard to express either in words or figures."

The strange part is how it started. In December 1900 Churchill was twenty-six and lecturing across America. Roosevelt — then governor of New York and vice president-elect — could not get to the New York lecture, and said so with real regret: "I am really sorry as I am a great admirer of Mr. Churchill's books, and should very much like to have a chance to meet him socially."

They dined at the Executive Mansion in Albany late that month. Something soured. Roosevelt's own account, seven months later: "I saw the Englishman Winston Churchill here and although he is not an attractive fellow, I was interested in some of the things he said."

They never met again. In 1910, sent to represent the United States at Edward VII's funeral, he wrote: "I have refused to meet Winston Churchill, being able to avoid any scandal by doing so."

Then, on 22 August 1914, to his English friend Arthur Lee: "I have never liked Winston Churchill, but, in view of what you tell me about his admirable conduct and nerve in mobilizing the Fleet, I do wish that if it comes your way you would extend to him my congratulations on his action."

Churchill seems never to have registered any of it. In 1918 he proposed sending Theodore Roosevelt to Moscow as the Allies' envoy to Lenin.
